source: Fleming & Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition
finding: Splits metacognition into bias, sensitivity and efficiency. Sensitivity is how well confidence separates correct from incorrect trials. Efficiency is sensitivity at a given task performance.
numbers: Efficiency is meta-d'/d'. A value of 1 is ideal; 0.7 means 30% of the evidence for the decision is lost when judging confidence.
quote: Metacognitive sensitivity is the separation between the distributions
limits: Raw sensitivity measures depend on task performance, so people or models on different tasks cannot be compared directly.
agent_relevance: Report confidence quality as discrimination (AUROC), apart from calibration (bias).

source: Fleming & Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition: type 2 ROC
finding: The type 2 ROC treats each confidence level as a criterion and plots hits against false alarms for being correct. Its area (AUROC2) is a bias-free sensitivity measure.
numbers: AUROC2 is affected by type 1 d' and by the type 1 criterion (Galvin et al. 2003, shown mathematically).
limits: AUROC2 changes with task difficulty even when metacognitive efficiency is unchanged.
agent_relevance: Compare AUROC of confidence across tasks only after checking difficulty; compare within a class.

source: Fleming & Lau (2014): calibration versus sensitivity
finding: Calibration (do 70% claims come true 70% of the time) is a separate property from sensitivity. A subject can be calibrated overall yet have no sensitivity.
numbers: Phi is the Pearson r between accuracy and confidence across trials; calibration curves show over- and underconfidence.
limits: Calibration needs many trials per bin.
agent_relevance: Track ECE and AUROC separately; a constant guess can have perfect ECE and zero AUROC.

source: Fleming et al. (2010) Relating introspective accuracy to individual differences in brain structure (Science)
finding: Founding human study. People differ a lot in how well confidence tracks correctness even when task accuracy is held equal. This ability maps onto anterior prefrontal structure.
numbers: N=32. Staircase kept accuracy at ~71% (range 70-74%). Confidence on a 1-6 scale. Metacognitive ability A_roc ranged 0.55-0.75. A_roc vs accuracy r=-0.11, p=0.56. Split-half reliability r=0.69, p=0.00001.
limits: Healthy volunteers, one visual task, structural MRI correlation, small N by current standards.
agent_relevance: Confidence quality is a stable trait, separate from skill; a model's skill does not imply self-knowledge.

source: Fleming et al. (2010) Science: brain structure results
finding: Gray matter volume in right anterior prefrontal cortex (BA10) predicted metacognitive ability but not task performance or overall confidence.
numbers: Peak [24,65,18], tmax=4.8, p<0.05 corrected. GM vs d': r=0.15, p=0.42. GM vs confidence bias B_roc: r=-0.023, p=0.90. Left inferior temporal gyrus correlated negatively (tmax=4.66). Left aPFC did not survive correction.
limits: Correlational. Replication across larger samples is needed; later work found the picture is domain-specific and distributed (see PMC5895040, not opened).
agent_relevance: Self-monitoring is a separate function from first-order decision making; in an agent it should be a separate pass or module.

source: Kiani & Shadlen (2009) Representation of confidence associated with a decision by neurons in the parietal cortex (Science)
finding: Monkeys could opt out for a small sure reward after seeing random-dot motion. Opt-out rate tracked difficulty. Parietal (LIP) neurons that carry the decision variable also carry certainty.
numbers: 70 LIP neurons from two monkeys in the population average; 19 neurons with sure-bet target in the receptive field. A three-parameter model fit the choices.
quote: the same neurons that represent formation of a decision encode certainty about the decision
limits: Two monkeys; sure-bet offered on a subset of trials; opt-out rather than a verbal rating.
agent_relevance: Opting out when unsure is a behavioural readout of confidence. A stopping rule can use it, if the signal is real.

source: Meyniel, Sigman & Mainen (2015) Confidence as Bayesian probability
finding: Cited as the framework that confidence is the probability of being correct given the evidence. Not opened this session.
numbers: none (not opened)
limits: Title-level knowledge only.
agent_relevance: Normative anchor: confidence should equal posterior probability of correct.

source: Fleming & Daw (2017) Self-evaluation of decision-making: a general Bayesian framework
finding: Confidence is a second-order inference on a coupled but distinct decision system, like judging another actor. First-order models use the same state for choice and confidence.
numbers: Simulations only. Accounts for confidence and error detection together, and for cases where metacognition is better or worse than task performance.
quote: computationally equivalent to inferring the performance of another actor
limits: Model, with few direct fits to new data in the paper.
agent_relevance: Treat self-evaluation as a separate inference with its own evidence (e.g. other samples), not as reading the answer's own state.

source: Fleming & Daw (2017): own actions as evidence
finding: The model predicts that one's own action contributes to confidence, so confidence can be biased by what was chosen.
numbers: Qualitative prediction from simulations.
limits: Needs behavioural tests of the prediction.
agent_relevance: Predicts choice-supportive bias in LLMs; see Kumaran et al. 2025.

source: Rollwage, Dolan & Fleming (2018) Metacognitive failure as a feature of those holding radical beliefs (Curr Biol)
finding: Radical-belief people showed lower metacognitive sensitivity on a neutral perceptual task and smaller confidence updates after disconfirming evidence. Key findings replicated in an independent sample.
numbers: Study 1 n=344 (survey). Study 2 n=381. Study 3 n=417 replicated key findings. Post-decision evidence set to 80% performance.
limits: Questionnaire-defined radicalism; correlational; US online samples.
agent_relevance: Weak sensitivity plus low updating is a failure pattern: the agent should update on contrary evidence.

source: Guo et al. (2017) On calibration of modern neural networks
finding: Modern deep nets are overconfident. Temperature scaling, a single parameter fit on held-out data, fixes most of it.
numbers: Example reliability plots show ECE 12.67 before and 0.96 to 2.46 after calibration on one panel; Table 1 reports ECE (%) with 15 bins; typical ECE 4 to 10% before.
limits: Image and document tasks, closed-class classification; fixed-distribution calibration.
agent_relevance: Calibration can be repaired cheaply on a hold-out set, within a class of problems.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large LMs are well calibrated on multiple choice when formatted right. Calibration improves with size and few-shot. The model can also judge its own sampled answers as P(True).
numbers: Models 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B. P(True)>0.5 samples were far more likely correct (Fig 1, five tasks). Showing the model many own T=1 samples improves P(True). 20-shot used.
quote: answers labeled with P(True) > 50% are far more likely to be correct
limits: Anthropic base models; 'None of the above' hurts calibration. Calibration is worse off distribution.
agent_relevance: Showing the model many of its own samples before judging one is the seed of sample-consistency.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022): P(IK) and RLHF
finding: A trained P(IK) head predicts whether the model knows the answer, partly transfers across tasks, but is poorly calibrated on new tasks. RLHF policies look miscalibrated, but one temperature (T=2.5) largely fixes it.
numbers: P(IK) rises with source material and with math hints in context. RLHF fix: same T=2.5 across evaluations.
quote: RL fine-tuning tends to collapse language model predictions towards behaviors that receive the most reward
limits: Authors say heavier RL might distort calibration beyond repair by temperature.
agent_relevance: Post-trained models need recalibration; do not assume base-model calibration holds.

source: Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 finetuned to say a confidence in words (CalibratedMath) gives calibrated numbers, also under distribution shift, and not just by copying logits.
numbers: Trained on Add-subtract, tested on Multiply-divide and Multi-answer. Table 1 gives MSE/MAD in percent; verbalized finetuned beat the constant baseline on MSE.
quote: first time a model has been shown to express calibrated uncertainty about its own answers in natural language
limits: Needs finetuning; arithmetic only; shift is moderate.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence can carry real information, when trained.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning
finding: Sample many reasoning paths and take the majority. Agreement with the majority is highly correlated with accuracy, so low agreement signals low confidence.
numbers: Gains: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%. LaMDA-137B GSM8K 17.1 to 27.7 (+10.6).
quote: self-consistency confers some ability for the model to know when it doesn't know
limits: Correlation shown on GSM8K (Fig 5); agreement is a hint, not a guarantee, because wrong answers can agree.
agent_relevance: Primary support for SCHEMA 4b: use sample agreement as the confidence signal.

source: Yin et al. (2023) Do large language models know what they don't know? (SelfAware)
finding: Builds SelfAware, a dataset of unanswerable questions in five categories with answerable pairs. Tests 20 LLMs for self-knowledge by detecting uncertainty in answers.
numbers: 20 LLMs, including GPT-3, InstructGPT, LLaMA. Exact scores not extracted.
limits: Opened the abstract and intro only; numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Gives a test for abstention on unanswerable items.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration (RLHF-LMs)
finding: For ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Claude 2, verbalized confidence is often better calibrated than token probabilities. ECE drops by a relative 50% or more.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, TriviaQA: label prob. ECE 0.140, AUC 0.869; Verb. 1S top-1 ECE 0.068, AUC 0.879; Verb. 1S top-4 AUC 0.896. SciQ: label prob. ECE 0.256, Verb 1S top-4 ECE 0.065. TruthfulQA: label prob. ECE 0.451, AUC 0.418 (below chance); verbalized AUC 0.455-0.551.
limits: Asking for several guesses then confidence (top-k) helps; on adversarial TruthfulQA all methods are near chance in discrimination.
agent_relevance: Verbalized confidence is better calibrated than logits, but discrimination is weak on hard items.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Black-box benchmark of prompts, sampling and aggregation on five LLMs and eight tasks. Verbalized confidence is overconfident and a poor failure predictor.
numbers: GPT-4 vanilla average AUROC 62.7% (50% is chance). GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE >0.377. About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4. White-box vs black-box gap: 0.522 to 0.605 AUROC.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident
limits: No strategy wins everywhere; all methods struggle on professional-knowledge tasks (law, ethics).
agent_relevance: Do not use stated confidence to stop; it is overconfident and weakly discriminative.

source: Xiong et al. (2024): CoT lowers ECE without better discrimination
finding: Lower ECE can come from higher accuracy, not better self-knowledge.
numbers: GPT-4 with CoT on GSM8K: 93.6% accuracy, ECE 0.064, by giving 100% confidence to every item. Confidences stayed at 80-100%.
limits: Illustrates a known flaw of ECE alone.
agent_relevance: Always check AUROC next to ECE.

source: Xiong et al. (2024): variance across samples helps
finding: Using the spread of M=5 sampled answers improves failure prediction over a single verbal rating.
numbers: GPT-3.5, CoT + consistency aggregation, M=5. Prompt (M=5) average ECE 18.7, AUROC 73.0; Self-Random (M=5) ECE 17.3, AUROC 69.6. GSM8K AUROC 88.6 to 92.7.
limits: M=5 samples cost 5x; gains are smaller on law and strategy tasks (AUROC ~60-66).
agent_relevance: Supports sample consistency (SCHEMA 4b), at a cost; still only a hint.

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty (semantic entropy)
finding: Entropy over meaning clusters of sampled answers predicts correctness better than token-level entropy. Sequence probabilities are misled by paraphrase.
numbers: Measured by AUROC on TriviaQA and CoQA; semantic entropy beat predictive entropy, normalised entropy, lexical similarity, and p(True) 'dramatically' (text claim). Exact AUROCs only in figures.
quote: semantic entropy has a significantly higher AUROC than entropy in sequence-probability-space
limits: Needs sampling and a meaning-equivalence check; free-form QA on OPT-family models.
agent_relevance: A form of sample consistency that groups by meaning. Suits an agent with a judge for equivalence.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know
finding: Prompting alone does not give good calibration. Finetuning on about a thousand graded examples (LoRA) gives better ECE and AUROC and transfers across models.
numbers: Models LLaMA-2 7B/13B, Mistral 7B, LLaMA-3, open-ended MMLU. Prompting ECE does not improve with a better base model; AUROC rises slightly but the best prompted model lags the worst finetuned one. A thousand graded examples suffice. User study included.
quote: prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration
limits: Needs weights and labelled data.
agent_relevance: Supports a class record of graded outcomes as a calibrator, outside the model.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs know and what people think they know (Nature Mach. Intell.)
finding: People overrate LLM answers when shown default explanations; longer explanations raise confidence without raising accuracy. Matching explanation wording to model confidence narrows both gaps.
numbers: AUC of model confidence: GPT-3.5 .751, PaLM2 .746 (multiple choice), GPT-4o .781 (short answer). Human AUC on default explanations .589, .602, .592. Aligning explanations: BF>100, 6.48, >100 across Expts 2a-c.
quote: longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy
limits: Online participants; three LLMs.
agent_relevance: Output length is not evidence of correctness (G10); do not let fluency drive trust.

source: Steyvers & Peters (2025) Metacognition and uncertainty communication in humans and LLMs
finding: Review that links human metacognition methods (confidence, sensitivity, calibration) to LLM tests and notes where they differ. Confidence is an overt expression of uncertainty.
numbers: No new data in the parts read.
limits: Review; the sections after the intro were not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Use human measures (separate bias from sensitivity) on agent confidence.

source: Kumaran, Fleming et al. (2025) Overconfidence in initial choices and underconfidence under criticism in LLMs
finding: Gemma 3, GPT-4o and o1-preview show choice-supportive bias when their earlier answer is visible, and overweight contrary advice versus Bayesian updating.
numbers: Change-of-mind rate: 32.5% (answer hidden) vs 13.1% (answer shown), coeff -3.4, p<0.0001. Opposite-advice weights -0.58 (shown) and -0.41 (hidden). Overweighting ratios of opposing advice 0.77, 0.92, 0.96 at advice accuracy 50, 60, 70%. Opposing vs same advice change rate 85.0% vs 39.2%.
limits: Latitude, SimpleQA, GSM-MC tasks; advice told to be 50-100% accurate.
agent_relevance: Showing the model its first answer anchors it; critique overshoots. Keep first-attempt confidence from fresh samples (S3 fresh context).

source: Ji-An et al. (2025) Language models are capable of metacognitive monitoring and control of their internal activations
finding: A neurofeedback-style paradigm shows LLMs can report and control only a few directions in their activations. The metacognitive space is much lower-dimensional than the neural space.
numbers: Depends on number of in-context examples, interpretability of the direction, and variance it explains. Control precision higher for earlier PC axes.
quote: LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations
limits: Open-weight models; synthetic task; not the same as confidence in answers.
agent_relevance: Self-report access is narrow, which is another reason for external consistency checks.
